content.title: Distance vs Displacement Explained
content.intro: When something moves, how do we measure how much it moved? Turns out there are two different answers, distance and displacement, and mixing them up is one of the most common mistakes in physics.

steps.narration: Distance is the total length of the actual path an object travels, no matter which direction it turns along the way.
Displacement, on the other hand, is the shortest straight line distance from the starting point to the final point, along with the direction.
Distance is a scalar quantity, it only has a magnitude, like five kilometres. Displacement is a vector quantity, it has both magnitude and direction, like three kilometres towards the east.
Let's say you walk four metres east and then three metres north. The total distance you walked is simply four plus three, which is seven metres.

But your displacement is the straight line from where you started to where you ended up. Using the Pythagorean theorem, that works out to the square root of four squared plus three squared, which is five metres.

Notice displacement, five metres, is smaller than distance, seven metres. In fact, displacement can never be greater than distance. At best, when you move in a straight line without turning back, the two become equal.
steps.display_text: Displacement is always less than or equal to distance

steps.narration: If you walk somewhere and then come all the way back to where you started, like a full lap on a circular track, your distance is the full length of the path, but your displacement is zero, because you ended up exactly where you began.

content.summary: Remember it this way, distance is how much ground you actually covered, while displacement is how far you ended up from where you started, in a straight line. Distance is always greater than or equal to displacement.
